The shot worked. It worked better than anything I'd tried in forty years.

Fifty-one pounds. My A1c the best it's been in a decade. And the food noise, the thing I could never explain properly to anybody, just quiet, for the first time since I was fourteen.

It wasn't that I wasn't drinking enough water. I was drinking a gallon a day and tracking it in an app.

It wasn't that I wasn't eating enough fiber.

It wasn't that I wasn't trying.

And when I finally found out what it actually was, I sat in my car in the hospital parking lot and cried. Which is the part that still embarrasses me.

I started the shot last October. By January, three months in, this was my normal.

Nauseous most of the day. Not from the medication directly. From being backed up.

Cramps that woke me up at night.

So bloated I caught myself in the elevator mirror at work and thought I looked pregnant.

And the one that was hardest to describe to anybody. The constant feeling of something in there that would not move.

I messaged my doctor. Told him I hadn't gone in six days and I was worried.

He said drink more water and add some fiber.

Then he moved on to my A1c.

So I did what everybody does. I bought the list.

Metamucil first. Then psyllium husk when the Metamucil did nothing. Miralax every morning stirred into my coffee. Magnesium citrate at night. Stool softeners, three a day. Prunes. Prune juice. Warm prune juice with butter in it, which is exactly as bad as it sounds.

And then eventually the thing nobody wants to admit they bought.

Some of it worked for a week. None of it worked for a month.

By March I was planning my life around it.

I cancelled a trip to see my daughter because I couldn't face four hours in a car and then a stranger's bathroom.

I got hemorrhoids for the first time in my life. Then a fissure. I'll leave that there.

And I started doing the arithmetic that everybody on this medication eventually does.

Fifty-one pounds. The best bloodwork of my adult life. Against not being able to go to the bathroom like a normal person.

I was seriously considering throwing all of it away.

That's the part I couldn't say out loud. Not to my husband. Definitely not to my doctor, because I knew exactly what he'd do. He'd cut my dose or take me off it.

So I said nothing. And I got worse.

It took a gastroenterologist I've worked beside for six years to explain it to me, and he did it in about ninety seconds standing at the coffee machine.

I'd made a joke about it. The kind of joke you make when something has stopped being funny.

He didn't laugh.

"What are you taking for it?"

I listed all of it.

"None of that's going to work."

I asked why.

"Because every one of those is treating what's in the pipe. Nobody's looking at the pipe."

He broke it down.

The medication slows your stomach. That's the mechanism. That's how it works. 

But when you slow the stomach you slow everything downstream. 

Your body produces fewer digestive enzymes, so food sits there and ferments instead of breaking down. 

Magnesium depletes because you're eating half of what you used to and absorbing even less than that. 

Bile production drops because bile only comes out when there's food to break down and you're barely eating. 

Motility suppresses, the actual squeezing that moves everything through your system, and it slows way beyond what the medication needs it to.

"So you've got a pipe with no lubrication, nothing pushing through it, and everything drying out and going hard. Then you put fiber on top of that." He shrugged. "Which is a bit like unblocking a toilet by pushing more paper down it."

I went home and sat on the edge of the bed with my coat still on.

Because it explained everything. Five months of it. The prunes. The gallon of water. The fissure. The trip I cancelled. All of it aimed at the wrong end of the problem.

Every single thing in my bathroom cabinet was designed to push from the bottom. Not one of them addressed why the system stopped working in the first place.

I didn't know what to do with that. So I did nothing for about three weeks and got quietly worse.

My daughter lives four hours away. She came down the last weekend in May since I'd been the one to cancel.

I tried to act normal. But I couldn't sit through dinner without shifting in my seat and she saw it.

"Mom. You're not okay."

And I told her all of it. The six days. The fissure. That I'd been thinking about stopping the medication and hadn't said it to anybody.

I hadn't cried in front of her since her father's surgery.

She didn't say much for a while.

Then she said, "I'm going to figure this out."

She's always been the one in our family who reads everything. Instruction manuals. Terms and conditions. Drug interaction labels. All of it.

She called five days later. She sounded like she was walking somewhere fast.

"Mom. I think I found something."

She drove back down that weekend with a container in her bag.

"Before you say anything," she said. "I know exactly what you're going to say. Just hear me out."

Here's what you should know about me. I am the last person alive who buys a supplement.

I have spent nineteen years watching patients bring me shopping bags of bottles they saw on Facebook.

And what's being sold to people on the shot right now is the worst of it. Half of it is the same fiber blend that was sold as a prebiotic three years ago with GLP-1 printed on the front in a new font. The rest is laxatives with a nicer label.

I said more or less that to her. Out loud.

She said, "I know. It isn't fiber and it isn't a laxative. That's why I brought it."

She sat down at my kitchen table and told me what she'd found.

"Everything you've been taking treats one symptom at a time. Miralax for the constipation. Ginger capsules for the nausea. Biotin for the hair. You've got six bottles for six problems and none of them are working because they're all treating symptoms of the same thing."

She sounded exactly like the gastroenterologist.

"Your medication slowed your entire system down. Magnesium is depleted, that's why nothing moves. Digestive enzymes dropped, that's why food sits there and you feel sick after eating. Bile production slowed, that's why the colon dried out. Electrolytes are off, that's why you're exhausted and foggy. It's one problem. One. And you've been throwing six separate things at it that each address maybe 10% of what's wrong."

She pushed the container across the table. Yellow label. KeepLean.

"This has all of it. The right magnesium, not citrate that just acts as a laxative, bisglycinate that actually absorbs. Ginger root for motility. Artichoke extract for bile flow. Digestive enzymes. Electrolytes. It's everything your body stopped getting when the medication changed how you process food. One scoop. Cold water. Every morning."

I looked at her.

"How much."

"About thirty dollars."

"Fine."

She smiled.

I started it the next morning. One scoop in cold water before work. It tasted like ginger beer, which annoyed me because I wanted a reason to not like it.

Nothing Tuesday. Nothing Wednesday.

Thursday morning I went. Not dramatically. Just easily. No straining. No bracing. Nothing else taken alongside it.

I was still skeptical. One time means nothing. But it was the first bit of hope I'd had since Christmas.

Week one I went three times.

I'd been going roughly three times in two weeks. So that number meant something to me that it wouldn't mean to anybody else.

Week two the bloating came down enough that I noticed my waistband before I noticed the scale. And the nausea that had been following me around for months went quiet. Not managed. Quiet. I ate lunch at work and went back to my desk without sitting with my head down for twenty minutes.

Week three the cramping stopped. I hadn't expected that at all because I'd decided the cramping was just the medication and I was stuck with it. I also realized I had energy past 5pm. I cooked dinner on a Wednesday. My husband looked at me like I'd come back from somewhere.

Week five I realized I'd stopped counting days.

For five months I'd had a number in my head at all times. What day I was on. How many days since the last time. I didn't decide to stop tracking it. I just noticed one morning that I didn't know the number anymore. Because it didn't matter anymore. Because I was going every morning like a normal person.

Last month I drove the four hours to my daughter's house. I didn't plan anything around it. I just went.

I had my follow-up in July.

Same doctor. The one who told me to drink more water.

He asked how I was getting on. I told him the truth for the first time in eight months. That I'd come within about two weeks of quitting his medication. That I hadn't told him because I was afraid he'd take it off me.

He was quiet for a second.

Then he asked what I'd changed.

I told him.

He wrote the name down on the back of a card.

Then he said, "I wish I'd known to tell you that eight months ago."

Me too.

Because if I'd known in January I'd have kept the trip. I wouldn't have the fissure. I wouldn't have spent five months lying to my own doctor about how bad it was.

That's why I'm putting this on the internet with my name on it.

If any of this is your life right now.

You're straining and nothing comes out.

You're counting days. You know exactly what day you're on right now.

You're backed up to the point where you're nauseous from it, not from the medication.

You've bought the entire list and nothing holds for more than a week.

You're so tired by 4pm that you can't function and everyone keeps telling you it's just the adjustment period.

And you've started doing the arithmetic. Asking yourself whether it's worth it.

Then let me save you the five months.

Almost everything sold to people on the shot is fiber with new packaging. Turn the bottle over and read it. If the first thing is psyllium or inulin or a prebiotic blend, that's the thing that made me worse.

The rest is laxatives with a nicer label. Senna. Smooth Move. Dulcolax. Those work the first time. Then they work less. Then you need more.

I prepped people for colonoscopies for eleven years. I've seen on a screen what taking one of those every day does. I wouldn't do it and I wouldn't let my mother do it.

KeepLean is not fiber and it's not a laxative. It addresses why the system stopped working, not just what's stuck inside it. Magnesium for the depletion. Ginger for the motility. Artichoke for the bile. Enzymes for the breakdown. Electrolytes for everything else that went sideways when you started eating half as much.

One scoop. Cold water. Every morning. That's the whole thing.

What I can tell you is it's the only thing in five months that changed anything.

I ordered three the next time round. Two for me because I'd worked out what happens if I run out and I wasn't willing to find out again. And one for a friend from church who's been on the shot since last spring.

She rang me about three weeks later. Crying.

She said, "I didn't realize how bad I'd been feeling until I stopped feeling like that."

There are four of us at my hospital on it now. All on the shot. Every single one of us had the same pile of stuff in the bathroom cabinet that wasn't working.

One of the nurses on my floor didn't order it when I told her about it. She meant to. You know how that goes.

She stopped the medication in April instead. She'd lost thirty pounds and her blood pressure was normal for the first time in years and she gave it up because she couldn't take one more week of this.

She's put nineteen of it back on.

She said to me last month, "I wish I'd just ordered it when you told me."

That's the one I think about. Not the bad days. The people who did everything right, finally got the thing they'd been chasing for years, and handed it back over something that had a fix nobody bothered to tell them about.

So that's it. That's all I wanted to say.

You're not failing at this. You were given the wrong instructions. Water and fiber is the right advice for ordinary constipation. This isn't ordinary constipation. This is a system that's been slowed down and depleted and nobody addressed the actual cause.

And you shouldn't have to choose between the medication that's finally working and being able to live in your own body.

If you try it and it does nothing, they give your money back. 60 days. That's the only reason I was willing to spend anything at all on it after the year I'd had.

content.body:
I spent 2 years working on a tirzepatide trial site.

I drew the labs. I logged the side-effect diaries. Then I spent 18 weeks logging myself, wearing a $65 bracelet.

I'm 55. Here is my n=1, next to what I recorded.

The Person Holding The Clipboard :

I'm Deborah. Clinical research nurse, 26 years, the last stretch of it on a site running a tirzepatide trial. Zepbound, as the world knows it now.

My job was the unglamorous truth of a drug trial. Blood draws at 7am. Weigh-ins on the calibrated scale. Sitting with participants while they filled out side-effect diaries, week after week.

So when I say I know what this drug does, I mean I physically recorded what it does.

And while I recorded it, my own belly was quietly staging its takeover. I'm 55. Menopause finished the job at 52, and 14 lbs settled directly on my middle over 2 years. I weighed participants all day and avoided scales at home. A research nurse, hiding from data. I'm aware of the irony.

The low point was a Tuesday in the supply room, changing into scrubs, when I realized I'd started ordering them a size up so the drawstring wouldn't dig a red line into my stomach by noon. I stood there holding the old pair and just felt tired.

What The Clipboard Says :

Let me be rigorous, because rigor is the only thing I have to offer you.

Tirzepatide is impressive. I'll say it plainly. In the published results, average participants lost around a fifth of their body weight over a year and a half. I watched versions of that happen in my own hallway. It is the most effective weight-loss medication I have ever seen up close.

Now the rest of my logbook.

The diaries I collected were full of nausea, constipation, and diarrhea, and GI misery was the main reason people dropped out at our site. Not vanity. Vomiting.

Around month 6, most of our participants' curves started flattening. The early free-fall becomes a slow negotiation. Nobody tells you that part in the commercials.

And the discussion that stuck with me most was about what happens after discontinuation. When people stop, much of the weight tends to come back within the year. The drug is a faucet, not a repair.

One more line for my own file: without insurance coverage, Zepbound runs about $1,059 a month. My coverage said no, twice. On a nurse's salary, that is not a decision. That is arithmetic.

Also, and this is the line that mattered most to my particular belly: tirzepatide works on appetite and blood sugar hormones. Not once, in 2 years of source documents, did I see it aimed at cortisol. My 3:15am wake-ups, my wired-but-exhausted afternoons, my stress-belly. Different mechanism. Different problem.

Enrolling Myself, n=1 :

A woman in my menopause group kept talking about an acupressure bracelet. I did what research nurses do. I was polite and believed none of it.

Then she repeated what her practitioner had told her, that her belly was cortisol, not calories, that stress drives cravings and slows metabolism, and something in me went quiet, because that matched my own labs better than any appetite story did.

$64.90 against $1,059 a month I couldn't access anyway. I enrolled myself in a study of one. Placebo or not, I decided I would at least log it honestly.

The Protocol I Ran On Myself :

Same scale, same tape measure, every Sunday at 7am, fasting. Old habits.

Week 1-2: primary endpoint, no change. Scale identical. Secondary observation: I slept through the night 4 times in week 2. Baseline: almost never.

Week 3: scale still flat. I nearly terminated the study early. My own diaries from the trial talked me out of it. Nothing honest works in 3 weeks.

Week 4-6: waistband data. My navy work pants closed without breath-holding. Down 4 lbs. The evening bloat, my most reliable symptom, dropped from daily to rare.

Week 7-12: down 9 lbs, 2 inches off my waist. I was walking after dinner and had stopped the 9pm stress-snacking, not through willpower, but because the pull just wasn't as loud. Credit where due: I did the work. The bracelet let the work count.

Week 13-18: 13 lbs total, 3 inches off my waist.

Results Table :

My n=1 vs what I logged for 2 years:

Cost: $1,059 a month without coverage vs $64.90 once
Average result: around a fifth of body weight, best drug I've ever charted vs my 13 lbs and 3 inches in 18 weeks
Side effects logged: nausea, vomiting, GI dropouts in my own files vs none in mine
Month 6: the curve flattens vs my sleep is still holding
After stopping: much of it returns within a year vs nothing to discontinue
Cortisol, the 3am axis: not the mechanism, never claimed vs the first thing that moved

Read that fairly. On raw pounds, the drug wins, and I would never dress that up otherwise. If you have coverage, a tolerant stomach, and a plan to stay on it long-term, Zepbound is a legitimate, remarkable tool.

I had none of those 3 things. I had a cortisol belly and $65.

Endpoints That Matter At 55 :

I'm down a full pants size. The tape says 3 inches. My sister, who measures nothing and notices everything, grabbed my waist at my niece's graduation party and said, "Where did you go?"

At my checkup, my doctor compared this year's waist measurement to last year's, raised an eyebrow, and said, "Keep doing whatever this is." That is as enthusiastic as medicine gets, and it's enough.

For external validity, I did what I do: I read the data I could find, about 1,100 verified reviews. The distribution matched my curve. Sleep early, waist late. The ones expecting week-1 miracles were the unhappy tail.

Investigator's Conclusion :

I still believe in the drug I helped study. If a friend qualified and could afford it, I'd hold her hand through the nausea weeks.

But I'd also tell her what 2 years of diaries taught me: there is no injection for cortisol, and for a lot of us at 55, cortisol is the belly.

My study of one is ongoing. The bracelet stays on.

👉 If Zepbound's price tag or your insurance already made the decision for you, run your own n=1 on the cortisol side of the problem. $64.90 at the official store, 30-day guarantee, log it honestly like I did.
